chapters.n: Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel in the 700s BC, during a time of prosperity under Jeroboam II, followed by chaos and the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC. He was a contemporary of Amos, Isaiah, and Micah.

f.g: Hebrew “salvation”—the same root as Joshua and Jesus.
Jeroboam II, king of Israel about 786–746 BC.

chapters.n: God commands Hosea to marry a woman who would prove unfaithful. His painful marriage becomes a living parable of God’s relationship with Israel, who had been unfaithful by worshipping other gods.

f.g: A woman inclined to unfaithfulness; scholars debate whether she was unfaithful before or after the marriage.

f.w: the land hath committed great whoredom
f.g: Idolatry is pictured as adultery against God, Israel’s covenant husband.

chapters.n: Hosea obeys and marries Gomer, who bears him a son.

f.g: Nothing else is known of her family.

chapters.n: The son is named Jezreel, recalling the valley where King Jehu’s dynasty began with bloodshed. Jehu had been commanded to end Ahab’s house, but his excessive violence brought judgment on his own line—fulfilled when Jeroboam II’s son was assassinated.

f.g: “God sows” (or scatters)—a name with both judgment and hope.

f.w: the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu

chapters.n: Israel’s military power (its “bow”) will be broken in the Jezreel Valley, a famous battlefield.

f.w: I will break the bow of Israel

chapters.n: Gomer bears a daughter—perhaps not Hosea’s, since the text no longer says “bare him.” She is named Lo-ruhamah, “not pitied” or “not loved,” because God would withdraw His compassion from Israel.

f.g: Hebrew “not pitied” or “unloved.”

chapters.n: Judah, however, will be shown mercy and saved by the Lord—not by armies. This was fulfilled when God delivered Jerusalem from Assyria in Hezekiah’s day.

f.w: not save them by bow, nor by sword

chapters.n: After weaning her daughter (often at two or three years), Gomer has another son.
He is named Lo-ammi, “not my people.” This reverses the covenant promise “I will be your God, and ye shall be my people”—the most painful name of all.

f.g: Hebrew “not my people.”

f.w: I will not be your God

chapters.n: Yet God immediately promises hope: Israel will become as countless as the sand of the sea, fulfilling the promise to Abraham. Those once called “not my people” will be called “children of the living God.” Paul and Peter apply this to all who come to Christ.

f.w: as the sand of the sea
Ye are the sons of the living God

chapters.n: Judah and Israel—divided since Solomon’s death—will be gathered together under one leader. Many see this as the future reunion of all Israel under the Messiah, the latter-day gathering. “Jezreel” now means God will plant His people again.

f.w: gathered together, and appoint themselves one head
great shall be the day of Jezreel
f.g: Jezreel—“God sows”—now points to God replanting His people.

chapters.n: Chapter 2 begins by reversing the children’s names: call your brothers Ammi (“my people”) and your sisters Ruhamah (“loved”). Some translations place this verse at the end of chapter 1, as the conclusion of its promise.

f.g: “My people”—Lo-ammi without the “not.”
“Pitied” or “loved.”

chapters.n: Now the Lord speaks like a wronged husband in court, urging the children to plead with their mother (Israel) to give up her unfaithfulness. The marriage is broken—but He still wants her back.

f.w: she is not my wife, neither am I her husband
f.g: Language resembling a divorce declaration, though the goal is reconciliation.
Argue a case, contend.

chapters.n: If she does not change, she will be stripped bare and left like a desert—a picture of the land’s devastation in war and drought.

f.w: set her as in the day that she was born

chapters.n: Her children, sharing her unfaithfulness, will share her fate. The people of Israel are both the wife and the children in this extended metaphor.
Israel credited her “lovers”—the Baal gods and foreign allies—for her food, clothing, and oil. Baal was the Canaanite storm god believed to give rain and fertility.

f.g: Baal and other gods (and perhaps foreign alliances) Israel trusted for prosperity.

chapters.n: God will block her path with a thorn hedge and wall, so she can’t find her way to her lovers. His “obstacles” are acts of love meant to turn her back.

f.w: I will hedge up thy way with thorns

chapters.n: Frustrated in chasing her lovers, she will say, “I’ll go back to my first husband; I was better off then”—like the prodigal son who came to himself.

f.w: I will go and return to my first husband

chapters.n: She never realized that it was the Lord who gave her grain, wine, and oil—and the silver and gold she used for Baal worship.

f.w: she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil

f.g: Used to make idols or offerings for Baal.

chapters.n: So God will take back His gifts at harvest time, showing who truly provides.

f.g: At harvest time, when she expects it.

chapters.n: He will expose her shame before her lovers, who will be powerless to rescue her.

f.g: Expose her shameful behavior.

chapters.n: Her celebrations will cease—festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths—because her worship had become empty and mixed with idolatry.

f.w: her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths

chapters.n: The vines and fig trees she called payment from her lovers will become wild thickets eaten by animals.

f.g: Wages, especially a harlot’s fee.

chapters.n: God will punish her for the feast days of the Baals, when she dressed up with jewelry to chase other gods and forgot Him. Forgetting God is the root sin.

f.g: Plural of Baal—the various local Baal gods.

chapters.n: Here the chapter turns. Instead of final rejection, God will woo Israel back, lead her into the wilderness as in the Exodus, and speak tenderly to her heart. This is the heart of Hosea’s message: God’s relentless, redeeming love.

f.g: Woo, persuade lovingly.
Literally “speak to her heart.”

chapters.n: The valley of Achor (“trouble”)—where Achan sinned and was punished—will become a door of hope. Israel will respond as she did as a young bride coming out of Egypt.

f.g: “Valley of Trouble.”

f.w: as in the days of her youth

chapters.n: Israel will call God Ishi (“my husband”) rather than Baali (“my master”)—a relationship of love, not mere ownership, and free from any confusion with Baal.

f.g: Hebrew “my husband.”
Hebrew “my master” or “my Baal”—a word also used for husband, but tainted by idolatry.

chapters.n: God will remove the names of the Baals from her lips; they won’t even be remembered.

f.w: I will take away the names of Baalim

chapters.n: God will make a covenant of peace with all creation and abolish war. Israel will rest securely—a picture of the Millennium.

f.w: make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field
I will break the bow and the sword

chapters.n: “I will betroth you to Me forever.” God offers a brand-new marriage covenant, with gifts of righteousness, justice, steadfast love, and compassion. In ancient times the groom paid a bride-price—here God Himself provides the gifts.

f.w: I will betroth thee unto me for ever

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed—loyal, covenant love.

chapters.n: He will betroth her in faithfulness, and she will “know the LORD”—an intimate, personal knowledge, the goal of the covenant.
In that day God will answer the heavens, and the heavens will answer the earth—a chain of blessing as rain falls again.

f.g: Or “I will answer.”

chapters.n: The earth will answer with grain, wine, and oil, and they will answer Jezreel (“God sows”). Everything Israel sought from Baal now comes from God.
God will “sow” Israel in the land, show mercy to Lo-ruhamah, and say to Lo-ammi, “You are My people,” and they will answer, “You are my God.” Every name of judgment is reversed into a name of grace.

f.w: I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people
I will sow her unto me in the earth
f.g: A play on Jezreel, “God sows.”

chapters.n: God tells Hosea to go again and love his wife, though she has been unfaithful—just as the Lord keeps loving Israel while they turn to other gods. Raisin cakes (KJV “flagons of wine”) were used in pagan festivals.

f.w: according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel

f.g: Better “cakes of raisins,” offered in Baal worship.

chapters.n: Hosea buys her back for fifteen shekels of silver plus barley—roughly the price of a slave. Gomer had apparently fallen into servitude, and Hosea pays to redeem her, a vivid picture of God redeeming His people at a cost.

f.g: Redeemed or purchased her freedom.
About 6 bushels—barley was a cheap grain.

chapters.n: Hosea sets a period of waiting: she must stay with him faithfully, without other men, and he will be faithful to her. Restoration involves a time of discipline and rebuilding trust.

f.w: Thou shalt abide for me many days
f.g: A season of probation before full marital restoration.

chapters.n: Likewise, Israel will live a long time without king, sacrifice, or religious objects—both legitimate ones (ephod) and illegitimate ones (sacred pillars, household idols). This describes Israel’s long exile and scattering.

f.g: A sacred standing stone or pillar.
A priestly garment used to seek God’s will.
Household idols.

chapters.n: Afterward Israel will return and seek the Lord and “David their king”—the Messiah from David’s line—coming to Him with reverent awe in the latter days. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the gathering of Israel to Christ.

The second part of Hosea (chapters 4–14) is a series of messages. God brings a legal case against Israel: there is no faithfulness, no loyal love, and no knowledge of God in the land—the three things the covenant required.

f.g: A lawsuit or legal dispute.
Hebrew ḥesed—loyal, covenant love.

chapters.n: The list of sins echoes the Ten Commandments: false swearing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery. Violence follows violence—“blood touches blood.”

f.w: swearing, and lying, and killing, and stealing, and committing adultery

f.g: One murder follows another.

chapters.n: Because of human sin, creation itself suffers—the land mourns and even animals, birds, and fish waste away. Sin affects the whole environment.

f.g: Waste away.

chapters.n: God says no one should blame others; His real complaint is against the priests. The KJV phrasing is obscure; many translations read, “My contention is with you, O priest.”

f.w: thy people are as they that strive with the priest
f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; it likely means God’s charge is against the priest.

chapters.n: Priest and false prophet will stumble day and night, and the nation (their “mother”) will be destroyed.

f.g: The nation of Israel, as in Hosea 2:2.

chapters.n: A famous verse: God’s people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. The priests rejected the knowledge of God they were supposed to teach, so God rejects them. Ignorance of God is deadly.

f.w: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge

chapters.n: The more priests there were, the more they sinned. God will turn their glory into disgrace.
The priests profit from the people’s sins—they eat the sin offerings, so they actually want people to keep sinning!

f.w: They eat up the sin of my people
f.g: The priests ate portions of sin offerings, so more sin meant more food for them.

chapters.n: “Like people, like priest”—both will be judged for their deeds. Religious office gives no immunity.
They will eat but never be satisfied, and their fertility rites won’t produce offspring—because they stopped heeding the Lord.

f.w: they shall eat, and not have enough

chapters.n: Immorality and wine take away understanding. Sin dulls the mind and heart.

f.g: Rob them of understanding or judgment.

chapters.n: God’s people ask advice from a piece of wood and seek direction from a stick—forms of pagan divination. A spirit of unfaithfulness has led them astray.

f.g: Wooden idols.
A divining rod used to seek omens.

chapters.n: They offer sacrifices on hilltops under shady trees—popular sites of Canaanite worship. Their daughters and daughters-in-law are drawn into the immorality connected with those rites.

f.w: under oaks and poplars and elms

f.g: Daughters-in-law (literally “brides”).

chapters.n: God will not single out the young women for punishment, because the men themselves are worse—consorting with cult prostitutes. A people without understanding will be ruined.

f.g: Cult prostitutes connected with fertility worship.

f.w: the people that doth not understand shall fall

chapters.n: A warning to Judah not to follow Israel’s example. Gilgal and Bethel (mockingly called Beth-aven, “house of wickedness”) had become centers of corrupt worship.

f.g: “House of wickedness”—a sarcastic name for Bethel (“house of God”).

chapters.n: Israel is as stubborn as a heifer that refuses the yoke. Can the Lord now pasture them like a lamb in an open meadow? (The question implies He cannot.)

f.g: A stubborn young cow.

chapters.n: Ephraim—another name for the northern kingdom—is joined to idols; “leave him alone.” Persistent sin can bring a point where God lets people go their own way.

f.g: The leading tribe of the north; Hosea uses it for the whole northern kingdom.

chapters.n: When their drinking is over, they turn to immorality. Their rulers love shame more than honor.

f.g: Their liquor is gone, or has turned sour; the Hebrew is difficult.

chapters.n: A wind will sweep them away in its wings—exile—and they will be ashamed of their sacrifices to false gods.

f.w: The wind hath bound her up in her wings
f.g: A whirlwind will carry them off—a picture of exile.

chapters.n: God summons priests, people, and the royal household to judgment. Their leaders have been like hunters’ traps at Mizpah and Mount Tabor—places where people were lured into false worship.

f.g: Probably Mizpah in Gilead, a site of corrupt worship.
A prominent mountain in Galilee, likely a shrine site.

chapters.n: The rebels have sunk deep into slaughter, yet God has repeatedly corrected them. The Hebrew here is difficult; it may refer to pagan sacrifices or to political violence.

f.w: the revolters are profound to make slaughter
f.g: The rebels are deep in slaughter; the Hebrew is uncertain.
One who disciplines or corrects.

chapters.n: God knows Ephraim completely; nothing is hidden from Him. Israel is defiled by unfaithfulness.

f.w: Israel is not hid from me

chapters.n: Their actions don’t allow them to return to God, because a spirit of unfaithfulness rules them and they don’t know the Lord. Habitual sin makes repentance harder.

f.w: They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God
f.g: Their deeds don’t permit them to return.

chapters.n: Israel’s pride testifies against it. Both Israel and Judah will stumble.

f.w: the pride of Israel doth testify to his face

chapters.n: They will come with flocks and herds to sacrifice, but won’t find the Lord—He has withdrawn. Ritual without repentance cannot reach Him.
They have betrayed the Lord and raised children who don’t know Him. A new moon festival (“a month”) will devour them and their fields.

f.g: Children raised outside the covenant, or illegitimate children—a picture of a faithless generation.
Possibly a new moon festival, or simply a short time.

chapters.n: Sound the alarm! The trumpet blasts warn towns in Benjamin—Gibeah, Ramah, and Bethel—of invasion. These towns lay on the border between Israel and Judah.

f.g: Shofar—a ram’s-horn trumpet used to signal alarm.

chapters.n: Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of punishment. God has made it certain among the tribes.
Judah’s leaders are like people who move boundary stones—stealing land. God will pour out His wrath like a flood.

f.g: Those who move property markers to steal land.

chapters.n: Ephraim is crushed in judgment because it was determined to follow worthless commands—human-made rules or idols instead of God’s word.

f.g: Possibly “vanity” or “filth” in the Hebrew—worthless idols or human decrees.

chapters.n: God will be like a moth to Ephraim and rot to Judah—slow, unseen decay eating away at them from within.
When they felt their sickness, they turned to Assyria and its “great king” for help instead of to God. But Assyria couldn’t heal them. King Menahem of Israel paid tribute to Assyria around 740 BC.

f.g: Probably “the great king”—a title, not a name.

chapters.n: God Himself will attack like a lion, tearing and carrying off prey, with no one to rescue. The deeper message: the Lord, not Assyria, controls their fate.

f.w: I will be unto Ephraim as a lion

chapters.n: God will withdraw to His place until they admit their guilt and seek His face. In their distress they will earnestly seek Him. God waits with purpose, longing for their return.

f.w: till they acknowledge their offence, and seek my face

f.g: Seek Me earnestly, diligently.

chapters.n: A call to return: “Come, let us return to the LORD.” The God who wounded will heal; the one who struck will bandage. Discipline and healing come from the same loving hand.

f.w: let us return unto the LORD
he hath torn, and he will heal us

chapters.n: “After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up.” Originally a promise of quick national recovery, many Christians see in it a foreshadowing of Christ’s resurrection on the third day.

f.w: in the third day he will raise us up

chapters.n: Let us press on to know the Lord. His coming is as certain as sunrise, and He will come like spring rains that water the earth. Seeking God brings refreshment.

f.w: if we follow on to know the LORD

f.g: Autumn and spring rains that made crops grow in Israel.

chapters.n: God answers with heartbreak: “What shall I do with you?” Their devotion vanishes like morning mist or early dew—gone by mid-morning. Shallow repentance does not last.

f.w: your goodness is as a morning cloud
f.g: “Goodness” is ḥesed—loyalty; theirs evaporates quickly.

chapters.n: So God cut them down through the prophets and their words of judgment. His judgments shine out like light—clear and unmistakable.

f.w: I have slain them by the words of my mouth

chapters.n: One of the Old Testament’s great verses: God wants loyal love more than sacrifice, and knowing Him more than burnt offerings. Jesus quoted it twice to correct those who valued ritual over compassion.

f.w: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice

chapters.n: “Like Adam” (the Hebrew can read either “like men” or “like Adam”) they broke the covenant and betrayed God. Some read “at Adam,” a town by the Jordan.

f.w: they like men have transgressed the covenant
f.g: Or “like Adam” or “at Adam” (a town near the Jordan).

chapters.n: Gilead, east of the Jordan, is a city of evildoers stained with bloody footprints.

f.g: A region east of the Jordan; here possibly a city in it.

chapters.n: Gangs of priests lie in wait like robbers to murder travelers on the road to Shechem—a city of refuge and worship. Religious leaders have become criminals.

f.w: murder in the way by consent
f.g: Many translations read “murder on the way to Shechem.”

chapters.n: God has seen something horrible in Israel: Ephraim’s unfaithfulness has defiled the nation.
Judah too has a “harvest” of judgment appointed—yet the closing phrase hints at future restoration when God restores His people’s fortunes.

f.w: he hath set an harvest for thee
I returned the captivity of my people
f.g: When I restore the fortunes of My people.

chapters.n: Whenever God tried to heal Israel, more sin came to light. Samaria, the capital, was full of deceit, burglary, and street robbery.

f.w: When I would have healed Israel

f.g: Capital city of the northern kingdom.

chapters.n: They never stop to think that God remembers all their evil. Their deeds now surround them, in full view of God.

f.w: they consider not in their hearts that I remember all their wickedness

chapters.n: Court officials entertain the king with wickedness and lies. Corruption flows from the top down.
They are all burning with passion like a baker’s oven, so hot the baker doesn’t even need to stoke it while the dough rises. Their plotting smolders constantly.

f.w: as an oven heated by the baker
f.g: Ancient ovens were kept smoldering overnight and stoked to full heat in the morning.

chapters.n: On the king’s festival day, the officials get him drunk and he joins hands with mockers—setting the stage for a coup.

f.g: The heat of wine.
Mockers, arrogant scoffers.

chapters.n: Their hearts smolder with intrigue all night like an oven; by morning, the plot blazes into action.
Hot like ovens, they consume their rulers; king after king falls. In Hosea’s day, four of Israel’s last six kings were assassinated—yet no one calls on God.

f.w: there is none among them that calleth unto me

chapters.n: Ephraim mixes with the nations—adopting foreign ways and alliances. He is like a flat cake burned on one side and raw on the other: half-baked and useless.

f.g: Bread cooked on hot stones had to be flipped; unturned, it was charred and doughy.

chapters.n: Foreigners drain his strength, but he doesn’t notice. Gray hairs appear, but he doesn’t realize he’s growing old and weak. Spiritual decline can be gradual and unnoticed.

f.w: gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not
f.g: Decline creeping in unnoticed.

chapters.n: Israel’s pride testifies against it; despite everything, they will not return to the Lord.

f.w: the pride of Israel testifieth to his face

chapters.n: Ephraim is like a silly, senseless dove, flitting back and forth between Egypt and Assyria for help instead of trusting God. Israel’s last kings did exactly this.

f.g: A naive, easily misled dove; “heart” = sense.

f.w: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria

chapters.n: As they fly about, God will throw a net over them and bring them down like birds. Their schemes will catch them.

f.w: I will spread my net upon them

f.g: As they were warned in their assembly.

chapters.n: Woe to them! They fled from God and rebelled. He longs to redeem them, but they slander Him.
They wail on their beds but don’t cry to God from the heart. They gather to plead for grain and wine (perhaps through pagan rites) but turn away from Him.

f.w: they have not cried unto me with their heart
they assemble themselves for corn and wine
f.g: Some manuscripts read “they gash themselves,” a pagan practice to win rain.

chapters.n: God trained and strengthened them like a coach, yet they plot evil against Him.

f.g: Trained and strengthened them.

chapters.n: They turn, but not upward to the Most High—like a faulty bow that misses its mark. Their leaders will fall for their arrogant words, and Egypt will mock them.

f.g: A warped bow that cannot shoot straight.
Mockery.

chapters.n: Sound the alarm! An enemy swoops like an eagle (or vulture) over the Lord’s land, because Israel has broken His covenant and law. Assyria is coming.

f.w: Set the trumpet to thy mouth

f.g: Or vulture—a bird of prey descending.
Here the land or people of Israel, God’s household.

chapters.n: In trouble, Israel cries, “My God, we know You!” But their claim is empty; their lives show they don’t.
Israel has thrown away what is good, so enemies will chase them.
They made kings without consulting God and made idols with their silver and gold—to their own destruction. Israel’s last kings came to power by assassination, not God’s choosing.

f.w: They have set up kings, but not by me

chapters.n: God rejects Samaria’s calf idol. “How long will they be incapable of innocence?” Jeroboam I had set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan.
A craftsman made it, so it can’t be God. The calf of Samaria will be smashed to pieces. Idols are only as powerful as their makers.

f.w: the workman made it; therefore it is not God

chapters.n: A famous proverb: they sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind. Their foolish choices will produce a harvest of destruction far greater than what they planted. Even what grows will be eaten by foreigners.

f.w: they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind

f.g: Flour.

chapters.n: Israel is swallowed up and becomes, among the nations, like a useless pot that no one wants.

f.w: a vessel wherein is no pleasure

chapters.n: They went to Assyria like a wild donkey wandering alone. Ephraim pays for allies like hiring lovers—an especially shameful picture.

f.w: a wild ass alone by himself
f.g: A stubborn, wandering donkey; a pun on Ephraim (pere’ = wild donkey).

chapters.n: Though they bargain with the nations, God will gather them for judgment, and they will begin to suffer under the burden imposed by the “king of princes”—the Assyrian emperor’s heavy tribute.

f.g: The Assyrian emperor, who called himself king of kings.

chapters.n: Ephraim built many altars to deal with sin—but they became places for sinning. Religion without obedience multiplies guilt.
God wrote out His law for them in great detail, yet they treated it as foreign—something irrelevant to them.

f.w: I have written to him the great things of my law

f.g: Something foreign or alien.

chapters.n: They offer sacrifices and eat the meat, but the Lord doesn’t accept them. He will remember their sins and send them back to “Egypt”—into bondage again.

f.g: A symbol of renewed slavery and exile.

chapters.n: Israel forgot its Maker and built palaces; Judah built fortified cities. God will send fire on them. Trusting in buildings and defenses instead of God is futile.

f.w: I will send a fire upon his cities

f.g: Or “palaces.”

chapters.n: Perhaps spoken at a harvest festival: don’t celebrate like the pagan nations. Israel has been unfaithful, treating harvest as a reward from Baal on every threshing floor.

f.w: thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor
f.g: Prized grain at harvest as a harlot’s fee from Baal.
Threshing floor, where grain was separated at harvest.

chapters.n: The threshing floor and winepress will not sustain them; the new wine will fail.
They won’t remain in the Lord’s land. Ephraim will go back to “Egypt”—bondage—and eat ritually unclean food in Assyria. Exile meant losing the ability to live by the Law.

f.w: they shall eat unclean things in Assyria

chapters.n: In exile they can’t offer proper sacrifices. Their food will be like mourners’ bread—unclean because it was in a house of death. It will feed only themselves and never reach God’s house.

f.g: Food in a house where someone died was ritually unclean.

chapters.n: What will they do on the festival days, far from the land and temple, unable to celebrate?

f.g: An appointed festival.

chapters.n: Fleeing destruction, they will die in Egypt and be buried at Memphis—famous for its huge cemeteries. Weeds and thorns will overgrow their treasured homes.

f.g: An ancient Egyptian capital known for its necropolis (city of tombs).
Weeds with stinging hairs.

chapters.n: The days of punishment have come. The people mock the prophet as a fool and the inspired man as a madman—because their sin and hostility run so deep.

f.w: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad

f.g: A time when God comes to judge.

chapters.n: The prophet is meant to be Ephraim’s watchman with God, but people set traps for him everywhere, even in God’s house. Hostility to the prophet is hostility to God.

f.g: A bird-catcher’s trap.

chapters.n: Their corruption is as deep as at Gibeah, where a horrifying crime once led to civil war. God will remember and punish.

f.w: as in the days of Gibeah

chapters.n: God fondly remembers finding Israel long ago—like grapes found in the desert or the first ripe figs, a delightful surprise. But at Baal-peor they devoted themselves to shameful idolatry and became as vile as what they loved.

f.g: A rare, refreshing delight.
They became like the thing they loved.

chapters.n: Ephraim’s glory—its children and future—will fly away like a bird. No births, no pregnancies, no conceptions. Ephraim’s name relates to fruitfulness, making this especially pointed.

f.w: their glory shall fly away like a bird
f.g: Ephraim means “doubly fruitful”—now that fruitfulness will vanish.

chapters.n: Even if they raise children, they will lose them. Worst of all: woe to them when God departs!

f.w: woe also to them when I depart from them

chapters.n: Ephraim was planted in a pleasant place like Tyre, but will bring out its children to be slaughtered.

f.g: Tyre, a wealthy, beautifully situated Phoenician city.

chapters.n: Hosea, agonized, prays: what should You give them? Better barren wombs than children born only to die in war. This is a cry of grief, not cruelty.

f.w: a miscarrying womb and dry breasts

chapters.n: Their wickedness centers at Gilgal, a place of corrupt worship. There God came to “hate” them—reject them—and will drive them from His house. Their leaders are rebels.

f.g: Rebels.

chapters.n: Ephraim is struck like a plant whose root is dried up—no more fruit. Even their beloved children will perish.

“My God” will reject them because they did not listen; they will become wanderers among the nations. This describes the scattering of the northern ten tribes after 722 BC—whom Latter-day Saints believe God will gather again.

f.w: they shall be wanderers among the nations

f.g: Hosea speaks personally: Israel has rejected Him, but He is still Hosea’s God.

chapters.n: Israel is a vine that produces fruit only for itself. As prosperity grew, so did their altars and sacred pillars—they used God’s blessings to serve idols.

f.g: Possibly “a luxuriant vine”—fruitful but self-serving.
Fine sacred pillars used in idol worship.

chapters.n: Their heart is divided—or “slippery,” deceitful. They must bear their guilt, and God will tear down their altars and smash their pillars.
Soon they will say, “We have no king, because we did not fear the Lord—and what could a king do for us anyway?” Their political system has collapsed in futility.
Their promises are empty, their treaties made with false oaths. Lawsuits spring up like poisonous weeds in a plowed field.

f.g: A poisonous weed.

chapters.n: Samaria’s people will tremble for the calf idol at Beth-aven (Bethel). Its priests will wail as its glory is carried away.

f.g: Hebrew kemarim—a word used only for idol priests.

chapters.n: The calf will be carried to Assyria as a gift for the great king. What Israel worshipped becomes tribute for its conqueror—Ephraim will be put to shame.

f.g: “The great king”—the Assyrian emperor.

chapters.n: Samaria’s king will float away like a twig on water—powerless and gone.

f.w: as the foam upon the water
f.g: Like a chip of wood or foam swept away.

chapters.n: The shrines of wickedness will be destroyed and overgrown with thorns. People will beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them—words Jesus and John later used for future judgment.

f.w: they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us

f.g: “Wickedness”—short for Beth-aven (Bethel).

chapters.n: Since the days of Gibeah, Israel has kept on sinning. Gibeah’s war against the wicked didn’t stop sin from continuing in Israel.
God will discipline them when He chooses; nations will gather against them for their “double guilt.”

f.g: Probably “their double iniquity”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: Ephraim was like a trained heifer that enjoyed threshing grain—easy work where she could eat freely. Now God will put a yoke on her neck for hard plowing. Judah and Jacob will labor too.

f.w: loveth to tread out the corn
f.g: Threshing oxen could eat as they worked.

f.w: I passed over upon her fair neck
f.g: I will put a yoke on her neck.

chapters.n: A beautiful call to repentance: sow righteousness, reap the fruit of loyal love, break up the hard, unplowed ground of your hearts. It is time to seek the Lord until He comes and showers righteousness on you.

f.g: Plow unused, hardened soil—soften your hearts.

f.w: it is time to seek the LORD

chapters.n: Instead, they plowed wickedness and reaped injustice, eating the fruit of lies, because they trusted in their own way and their army.

f.w: Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity
the multitude of thy mighty men

chapters.n: War will break out, and all their fortresses will fall—like Shalman’s brutal destruction of Beth-arbel, where mothers and children were dashed to pieces. The event is otherwise unknown; Shalman may be a Moabite king or an Assyrian ruler.

f.g: Possibly Shalmaneser V of Assyria or Salamanu, a Moabite king; uncertain.
A town, perhaps in Gilead; location uncertain.

chapters.n: This will happen because of Bethel’s great wickedness. At dawn the king of Israel will be completely cut off—fulfilled when Hoshea, Israel’s last king, was taken prisoner by Assyria.

f.w: the king of Israel utterly be cut off

chapters.n: One of the tenderest chapters in the Bible. God speaks as a loving parent: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and called My son out of Egypt.” Matthew sees this pattern fulfilled when the child Jesus returned from Egypt.

f.w: called my son out of Egypt
When Israel was a child, then I loved him

chapters.n: The more God (through His prophets) called them, the further they wandered—offering sacrifices to the Baals and burning incense to idols.

f.w: As they called them, so they went from them
f.g: The more they were called, the more they turned away.
The Baals—local Canaanite gods.

chapters.n: Like a parent teaching a toddler to walk, God held Ephraim by the arms—yet they never realized it was He who healed them.

f.w: I taught Ephraim also to go
f.g: I taught Ephraim to walk.

f.w: they knew not that I healed them

chapters.n: God led them with gentle cords of human kindness and love. He was like someone who lifts a yoke off an animal’s neck and bends down to feed it. God’s leadership is loving, not harsh.

f.w: I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love

f.g: I bent down and fed them.

chapters.n: Because they refused to return to God, they will not go back to Egypt—instead Assyria will rule them.

f.w: the Assyrian shall be his king

chapters.n: War will rage through their cities and destroy them, because of their own schemes.

f.g: Possibly “gate bars” or “boasting priests”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: God’s people are determined to turn away. They are called upward to the Most High, but none will lift Him up.

f.g: Determined to turn away.

chapters.n: The emotional climax of Hosea: “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over?” Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom. God’s heart recoils; His compassion is stirred. Divine love wrestles with justice.

f.w: How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?

f.g: My compassion grows warm and tender.

chapters.n: God will not carry out His fierce anger or destroy Ephraim completely, “for I am God, and not man.” Human anger seeks revenge; God’s holiness includes mercy that endures.

f.w: for I am God, and not man
the Holy One in the midst of thee

chapters.n: A future gathering: they will follow the Lord, who roars like a lion to call His children home. They will come trembling from the west.

f.w: he shall roar like a lion
the children shall tremble from the west

chapters.n: They will come swiftly like birds from Egypt and doves from Assyria, and God will settle them in their homes—a promise of the gathering of Israel.

f.w: I will place them in their houses

chapters.n: Ephraim surrounds God with lies and deceit. Judah is described as still walking with God, though the Hebrew may mean Judah too is unruly; translations differ. (In many Bibles, this verse begins chapter 12.)

f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; some translations read “Judah still wanders from God.”

chapters.n: Ephraim chases the wind—the scorching east wind that brings only ruin. It multiplies lies and violence, making treaties with Assyria while sending olive oil as gifts to Egypt. Playing both sides was empty and dangerous.

f.g: Olive oil sent as tribute or bribe to secure an alliance.

chapters.n: God also has a case against Judah, and will repay “Jacob”—all Israel—for its ways.

f.g: A legal case, lawsuit.

chapters.n: Hosea recalls their ancestor Jacob, who grabbed his brother’s heel in the womb and, as a man, struggled with God. Like their father, the nation has been a grasping schemer.

f.w: He took his brother by the heel in the womb

chapters.n: Jacob wrestled with the angel and prevailed—but notice how: he wept and begged for a blessing. At Bethel God met him and spoke with “us”—his descendants too. Jacob’s true strength was in humble pleading.

f.w: he wept, and made supplication unto him

chapters.n: This God is the LORD, the God of hosts; “the LORD” (Jehovah) is the name by which He is to be remembered. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.g: His name of remembrance is YHWH (Jehovah).

chapters.n: Like Jacob, Israel must return to God, practice loyal love and justice, and wait on Him continually. This is Hosea’s message in a nutshell.
Israel has become like a dishonest trader with rigged scales who loves to cheat. The Hebrew word for merchant is “Canaanite”—Israel has become like the people they displaced.

f.g: Hebrew kenaʿan—“Canaan” or “trader.”

chapters.n: Ephraim boasts: “I’m rich! I earned it all myself, and no one can find any wrongdoing in me.” Wealth has blinded them to their sin.

The Lord, who has been Israel’s God since Egypt, will make them live in tents again—as in the wilderness or at the Feast of Tabernacles. It is both a judgment (losing their homes) and a hope (a fresh start with God).

f.w: make thee to dwell in tabernacles

chapters.n: God spoke through the prophets, gave many visions, and taught through parables and symbols. Israel had no lack of guidance.

f.w: I have also spoken by the prophets

f.g: Parables, comparisons, symbolic actions.

chapters.n: Gilead is full of wickedness and emptiness; Gilgal’s sacrifices of bulls are worthless. Their altars will become piles of stones in plowed fields—a pun on Gilgal and the Hebrew word for stone heaps (gallim).

f.g: Hebrew gallim—a wordplay on Gilgal.
Emptiness, worthlessness.

chapters.n: Jacob fled to Aram (Syria) and served as a shepherd to earn his wives. Hosea reminds them of their humble origins.

f.w: Jacob fled into the country of Syria

chapters.n: By a prophet—Moses—the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt and cared for them. In contrast to Jacob’s labor for a wife, God worked through prophets to save His people. Israel should listen to prophets now too.

f.w: by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt

chapters.n: Ephraim has bitterly provoked God. Their bloodguilt will remain on them, and the Lord will repay their contempt.

f.w: shall he leave his blood upon him
f.g: He will hold them responsible for their bloodshed.

chapters.n: Once, when Ephraim spoke, others trembled—it was the leading tribe. But when it became guilty through Baal worship, it “died” spiritually and politically.

f.w: when he offended in Baal, he died

chapters.n: They keep sinning more and more, making metal idols by their own design. People even say, “Let those who sacrifice kiss the calves!”—humans kissing idols in worship.

f.g: Idols made from melted, cast metal.
Kissing an idol was an act of worship.

chapters.n: So they will vanish like morning mist, early dew, chaff blown from a threshing floor, or smoke from a window. Four images of things that disappear quickly.

f.g: A window or opening that let smoke out.

chapters.n: “I am the LORD your God since Egypt; you know no God but Me, and there is no Savior except Me.” Latter-day Saints understand this Savior, Jehovah, to be Jesus Christ.

f.w: there is no saviour beside me

chapters.n: God cared for them in the desert, a land of terrible drought.

f.w: I did know thee in the wilderness
f.g: “Knew” suggests intimate care.

chapters.n: When they had good pasture, they were satisfied; when satisfied, they became proud and forgot God—a cycle repeated throughout scripture, and called the “pride cycle” in the Book of Mormon.

f.w: their heart was exalted; therefore have they forgotten me

chapters.n: So God will be like a lion and a leopard lurking beside the road.

f.w: I will be unto them as a lion

chapters.n: Like a bear robbed of her cubs, He will tear them open. The fierce images show how serious covenant betrayal is.

f.w: a bear that is bereaved of her whelps

f.g: Enclosure—the chest around the heart.

chapters.n: “O Israel, you have destroyed yourself; but in Me is your help.” Their ruin is self-inflicted; their only rescue is God.

f.w: thou hast destroyed thyself; but in me is thine help

chapters.n: Where is your king now to save you? Where are the rulers you demanded? God offers Himself as their true King.

f.w: Give me a king and princes

f.g: Many translations read “Where now is your king?”

chapters.n: God gave them a king in anger—beginning with Saul—and took kings away in wrath. Their last king, Hoshea, was captured by Assyria.

f.w: I gave thee a king in mine anger

chapters.n: Ephraim’s guilt is wrapped up and stored away, kept on record like a document tied and sealed. It will not be forgotten.

f.g: Tied up and preserved, like a sealed document.

chapters.n: Labor pains have come for rebirth, but Ephraim is an unwise child who won’t come out of the womb when it’s time. The nation refuses the new birth repentance offers.

f.w: The sorrows of a travailing woman
he should not stay long in the place of the breaking forth of children
f.g: He doesn’t present himself at the moment of birth.

chapters.n: A sudden burst of hope: “I will ransom them from the grave and redeem them from death. O death, where are your plagues? O grave, where is your sting?” Paul quoted this as a triumph song of Christ’s resurrection.

f.w: I will ransom them from the power of the grave
O death, I will be thy plagues
repentance shall be hid from mine eyes
f.g: Possibly “compassion is hidden from My eyes”—the Hebrew is debated.

chapters.n: Though Ephraim (“fruitful”) thrives among his brothers, a scorching east wind from the Lord will dry up his springs. The plunderer will take all his treasures—Assyria, sweeping in from the east.

f.g: The hot desert wind—an image of Assyria.

chapters.n: Samaria will bear its guilt for rebelling against God, and suffer the horrors of ancient war. Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC after a three-year siege.
Hosea’s final plea: “O Israel, return to the LORD your God, for your sin has made you stumble.” The book ends not with doom but with an invitation.

f.w: return unto the LORD thy God

chapters.n: Hosea even gives them the words to say: “Take away all our sin, receive us graciously, and we will offer the fruit of our lips”—praise instead of animal sacrifice.

f.g: Come with sincere words of confession.
Praise offered in place of bulls; the Greek reads “the fruit of our lips.”

chapters.n: True repentance means turning from false securities: Assyria (political alliances), horses (military power), and idols. In God the fatherless—the helpless—find mercy.

f.g: Asshur = Assyria.

f.w: we will not ride upon horses
in thee the fatherless findeth mercy

chapters.n: God answers: “I will heal their unfaithfulness; I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away.” Grace freely given is God’s final word in Hosea.
God will be like the dew to Israel—gentle, daily refreshment in a dry land. Israel will blossom like a lily and send down roots like the cedars of Lebanon.

f.w: I will be as the dew unto Israel

f.g: Famous for its majestic, deep-rooted cedars.

chapters.n: His shoots will spread, his beauty like an olive tree, his fragrance like Lebanon’s forests. The images of Ephraim as a withered plant are now reversed.

f.w: his beauty shall be as the olive tree

chapters.n: People will again live in his shade; they will flourish like grain and blossom like a vine, renowned like Lebanon’s wine.

f.w: they shall revive as the corn
f.g: Flourish like grain.

chapters.n: Ephraim will say, “What have I to do with idols anymore?” God replies, “I answer and watch over you. I am like a green cypress; your fruit comes from Me.” Only here in scripture is God compared to a tree—the evergreen source of every good thing.

f.w: What have I to do any more with idols?
From me is thy fruit found

f.g: An evergreen cypress or juniper.

chapters.n: An epilogue for every reader: whoever is wise will understand these things. The Lord’s ways are right; the righteous walk in them, but rebels stumble over them. The same path leads some to life and trips up others, depending on the heart.

f.w: the ways of the LORD are right
